source_title: Joseph Schlitz Brewing Company - decline after accelerated batch fermentation process change (Wikipedia, citing contemporaneous press)
publisher_issuer: Wikipedia (tertiary, citing contemporaneous reporting); corroborated by VinePair and The Beer Connoisseur retrospectives
company_context: Joseph Schlitz Brewing was the number-two US brewer as late as 1976. To cut cost and brewing time, Schlitz adopted an 'accelerated batch fermentation' (ABF) process and reformulated the beer (corn-syrup adjuncts, silica-gel haze prevention, high-temperature fermentation, cheaper extracts), cutting brewing time from roughly 25 days toward 15 days versus 32-40 days for Budweiser. The reformulated beer lost flavor and consistency, spoiled faster, and triggered a quality/trust collapse.
business_type: Mass-market brewing; brand-trust- and quality-consistency-dependent consumer product
company_size_stage: large national brewer (number-two US share in mid-1970s)
macro_context: Intense competition among Anheuser-Busch (Budweiser), Miller, Pabst, and Heileman; consumer sensitivity to beer taste and consistency.
evidence_summary: Seeking lower cost and faster throughput, Schlitz changed its formula and adopted accelerated batch fermentation, shortening brew time and substituting cheaper ingredients. The result was a hazy, flat, faster-spoiling product that drinkers rejected; a 1976 recall of more than 10 million cans and bottles (reported cost over $1.4 million) compounded the damage. Sales fell roughly 75% between 1976 and 1981, Schlitz dropped from the number-two US brewer toward fourth as Miller and Pabst passed it, and it closed its Milwaukee brewery in 1981 before being acquired. This is a self-inflicted quality/trust failure caused by a deliberate cost-driven process change.

source_backed_metrics.process_change: accelerated batch fermentation (ABF), brewing time cut from about 25 days toward about 15 days
source_backed_metrics.recall_volume: more than 10 million cans and bottles
source_backed_metrics.market_rank_change: from #2 (1976) toward #4 by early 1980s (passed by Miller and Pabst)

owner_decision_context: Management prioritized lower unit cost and faster production throughput, accepting a reformulation and accelerated process that compromised the taste, stability, and consistency that underpinned the brand's trust.
action_taken: Reformulated the beer and adopted accelerated batch fermentation to cut cost and brewing time; followed by a 1976 recall when product quality failed, with no early reversal of the underlying process decision.
outcome_evidence: Roughly 75% sales decline from 1976 to 1981, fall from number-two to fourth in US brewing, a multi-million-unit 1976 recall, and the 1981 closure of the Milwaukee brewery confirm the process/formula change destroyed brand trust and demand.
source_limitations: WebFetch of Wikipedia and trade retrospectives returns HTTP 403 here; figures verified from search snippets of Wikipedia and named trade outlets (VinePair, The Beer Connoisseur), which are retrospective secondary accounts of 1970s events rather than audited filings. The roughly 75% decline and recall figures are widely and consistently reported but originate from secondary sources.
